cues.text: A Deacon Called to the Papacy
Little is known with certainty of Leo's birth or early years beyond that he was of Roman or Tuscan origin.
Before his election as pope, he rose to the important office of archdeacon of Rome.
He was already trusted with delicate diplomatic missions on behalf of the Church before he himself sat on Peter's chair.
Elected pope in 440 while away on one such mission — reconciling two feuding Roman generals in distant Gaul — Leo inherited a Church facing a double crisis.
It would define his entire pontificate: a Western Roman Empire disintegrating under barbarian pressure, and an Eastern Church convulsed by a fresh Christological controversy.
This controversy was every bit as dangerous as the Arian and Nestorian crises that had come before it.
The Tome That Settled a Controversy
In the late 440s, a Constantinopolitan archimandrite named Eutyches sought zealously to guard against Nestorius's error of dividing Christ into two persons.
He swung to the opposite extreme, teaching that Christ's humanity had been effectively absorbed into his divinity, leaving only a single, blended nature.
Leo responded with a letter to the Patriarch of Constantinople, now known simply as the Tome of Leo .
It set out the Church's authentic teaching with remarkable clarity and balance: Christ is one Person existing in two complete and unconfused natures, divine and human.
Each retains its own properties while united, inseparably, in a single divine Person.
When this letter was finally read at the Council of Chalcedon in 451, the assembled bishops are recorded as crying out with one voice: Peter has spoken through Leo .
They recognized in the pope's careful formula the very heart of the apostolic faith itself.
Meeting Attila Outside Rome

In 452, with the Western Empire's military power a shadow of what it had once been, Attila the Hun led his forces into northern Italy, devastating cities as he advanced, with Rome itself apparently his next and most tempting target.
At the emperor's request, Leo traveled north with a small unarmed delegation to meet the feared conqueror in person near the River Mincio.
What exactly passed between pope and Hun in that meeting we cannot know with certainty; later legend added a vision of Saints Peter and Paul standing beside Leo, swords in hand.
But the historical fact is beyond dispute: Attila, against every expectation, agreed to withdraw from Italy and abandon his march on Rome, sparing the city a destruction it had every reason to fear.
Sparing Rome a Second Time
Leo's courage was tested again just three years later, in 455, when Vandal raiders under Genseric captured Rome itself.
Though Leo could not prevent the city's sack entirely, his personal intercession secured from Genseric a promise that the city would not be burned.

The inhabitants' lives, at least, would be spared — a partial but genuinely significant mercy wrung, once again, from a conqueror's hands by nothing more than a pope's own moral authority and personal courage.
Shepherd of a Universal Church
Beyond these dramatic confrontations, Leo governed the day-to-day life of the Roman Church and increasingly asserted the authority of the See of Peter over the wider Church.
His clarity would shape the papacy's self-understanding for the rest of its history.

In his many surviving sermons and letters, he insisted that the pope, as Peter's successor, bears a unique and enduring responsibility for the unity and orthodoxy of the whole Christian world, East and West alike.
Legacy
Leo died in Rome on 10 November 461, having guided the Church through a doctrinal crisis that could have permanently fractured Christian unity.
He also faced military threats that could have destroyed the city at the very heart of Western Christendom.
Declared a Doctor of the Church in 1754 and honored, alongside only one other pope, with the title "the Great," Leo remains the enduring image of the pope as both theologian and shepherd.

He was a man who could write, with unmatched precision, of the mystery of Christ's two natures, and who could also, when the moment demanded it, ride out unarmed to stand, quite literally, between his people and an invading army.
